High Processes Unsigned processes running from user-writable paths Tier 2
What was observed

1 process(es): payload.exe [PID 200] C:\Users\a\AppData\Local\payload.exe.

Why it mattersLegitimate software is normally installed under Program Files and signed. Unsigned executables running from AppData, Temp, or ProgramData match common malware staging behavior, but also match some legitimate updaters and developer tooling.

Suggested next stepSubmit the SHA-256 values in the artifact to threat intelligence, and check parent process and creation time for each.

High Security Defender real-time protection is disabled Tier 1
What was observed

Get-MpComputerStatus reports RealTimeProtectionEnabled = False.

Why it mattersReal-time protection off is both a common attacker action after gaining privilege and a common administrator misconfiguration. Correlate with Defender event IDs 5001/5007 to establish when and by what it was changed.

Suggested next stepCheck defender_operational.csv for configuration-change events around the disable time, and confirm whether a third-party AV legitimately took over.

High Security WDigest cleartext credential storage is enabled Tier 1
What was observed

HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\WDigest\UseLogonCredential = 1.

Why it mattersThis forces plaintext credentials into LSASS memory. It is not a default setting and is a well-documented pre-credential-theft modification.

Suggested next stepEstablish when this value was set and by which account. Treat credentials used on this host as potentially exposed.

Source artifact06_Security_Posture/hardening_registry_settings.csv

Info Collection Collection ran without Administrator rights Tier 1
What was observed

Coverage profile StandardUser as FIXTURE\user. 4 task(s) were skipped because they require an elevated token (see collection_coverage.json).

Why it mattersStandard-user collection still captures the current user's process list, readable network state, HKCU persistence, and profile artifacts. It does not capture the Security log, Prefetch copies, Amcache, SRUM, VSS, audit policy export, or other users' files. Missing those artifacts is a visibility gap, not evidence they were empty. Re-run elevated when the host owner can grant it.

Suggested next stepIf this is an incident, obtain an elevated collection or a disk/memory image. If this is a self-audit on a locked-down work PC, treat skipped tasks as out of scope and verify remaining artifacts against that user's activity only.

Methodology, Tiers, and Limitations

How to read the tiers

Tier 1 - Observed artifact. Directly present in the collected data, no interpretation applied. A registry value, an event ID, a signature status. State these as fact.

Tier 2 - Supported inference. A reasonable reading of one or more Tier 1 artifacts where other readings remain possible. An unsigned binary in AppData holding an outbound connection is consistent with C2 and equally consistent with a portable application. Cite the artifact and name the assumption.

Tier 3 - Unverified hypothesis. Not stated as findings by this tool. If you form one during analysis, record what evidence would move it to Tier 2.

Limitations of this collection
  • Live collection. Running this tool altered the host: a process was created, files were written, event log entries were generated, and prefetch and AmCache were updated. No memory image and no disk image were produced.
  • Point-in-time volatile data. Process, connection, and session data reflect the moment of collection only. Activity that ended before collection is absent from those artifacts.
  • Log retention bounds the window. Event data is limited to the configured window and to what retention preserved. Where a log was cleared, everything before that point is unavailable from this host.
  • Heuristics are not detections. The pattern lists used here match on common attacker tradecraft and also match legitimate administrative tooling. Expect false positives, and treat an empty findings list as an absence of matched patterns, not an absence of compromise.
  • Signature status is not integrity. A valid signature does not mean the binary is benign, and an invalid one does not mean it is malicious. Catalog-signed system files frequently return non-Valid status.
  • No anti-rootkit capability. All data is gathered through the operating system''s own APIs. Kernel-level tampering could render any of it unreliable.
  • Standard-user coverage. If this package was collected without Administrator rights, the Security log, Prefetch copies, Amcache, SRUM, VSS, secedit/auditpol, and other users'' artifacts were skipped by design. See 00_Collection/collection_coverage.json. Do not read those gaps as a clean host.
  • Timestamps. All times are UTC as reported by this host. Verify the host clock against the time source data before building a timeline, and note that file MACB times are trivially modifiable.
